target_customer: Small satellite and cargo operators needing low cost launch to orbit
problem: Small satellite operators lack cheap, frequent, flexible launch, and conventional rockets emit pollutants.
business_model: Launch services using a stratospheric balloon as first stage for a small rocket, with a planned in-orbit rocket network

founders.name: Sohrab Haghighat
prior_employers: Cruise (early employee, led Planning and Controls teams)
education: PhD in Aerospace Engineering (institution not listed)
founders.background_notes: YC page lists 13 patents and 23 papers.

founders.name: Saharnaz Safari
founders.background_notes: Named on the YC page as Haghighat's wife and co-founder; one article lists her as COO. Background not given.

exit.reason: Assignment in bankruptcy under section 49 of the Bankruptcy and Insolvency Act; Deloitte named trustee. Causes were not disclosed publicly. The YC page says the CEO later sold the IP.

competitors.name: Leo Aerospace
competitors.what: Balloon launched rocket (rockoon) for small satellites
competitors.traction_then: Test rockoon launched from Mojave desert in December 2018; planned first suborbital flight 2020

competitors.name: Zero2infinity
competitors.what: Bloostar balloon first stage launching ring rockets to orbit

technical_complexity.rationale: Needed a balloon launched rocket reaching orbit, new engines and in-orbit operations, which is hardware and regulatory heavy and had not been achieved by a small team.

defensibility.rationale: Patents and a built rocket factory and engine test setup would be hard to copy, but the company never reached orbit and balloon launch concepts were also pursued by others.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: No source shows an incumbent copying or buying SpaceRyde. Competition in small launch was crowded, and the company went bankrupt in 2023.

market_need_then: A June 2019 TechCrunch piece frames SpaceRyde as making access to space more available and affordable, and rockoon peers such as Leo Aerospace were launching tests in 2018 and 2019, indicating demand for small satellite launch.

branding.domain_note: Used spaceryde.com; company was founded as Loonify Space per SpaceQ and renamed SpaceRyde.

identity.voice_and_tone: Positions itself as a taxi to space and a rocket network; rocket named Ryder and balloon called Flying Spider.

branding.brand_signature: Taxi to space framing with the Ryder rocket and Rocket Network concept
branding.community_and_virality: Covered by TechCrunch, Yahoo, Global News and blogTO; CEO and COO pair covered as a husband and wife team competing with SpaceX; Chris Hadfield described as a mentor.

brand_strength.rationale: Reasonable regional press and a memorable taxi to space idea, plus a trademark portfolio, but no evidence of community or growth driven by the brand.

outcome_analysis: SpaceRyde reported about $10M raised from investors and government awards by mid 2022 and built a 25,000 square foot rocket factory, but did not reach commercial launch. SpaceNews tied the bankruptcy to local noise complaints that ended engine tests, and SpaceQ noted causes were not formally disclosed, with other pressures such as inflation and unclear balloon launch airspace rules. The company filed for bankruptcy on 2023-02-10 and the CEO later sold the IP.
